qs.q: To add a new node to an empty doubly linked list, you would ...

c.x: Set the first link equal to the new node and the last link to None.
Set the last link equal to the new node and the first link to None.
Set both the first and the last links equal to the new node.

e: In an empty list there is no node, so the new node is at the same time the first and the last node.
Both end references (first/head and last/tail) must therefore point to the new node, and the size becomes 1.
This is the same special case as enqueue on an empty linked queue (head = newest and tail = newest).
Leaving either end as None would make the list lose access to the new node from that end.

qs.q: The last node in a doubly linked list is often known as ____
e: The first and last nodes of a linked list are known as the head and the tail of the list.
In the doubly linked list of the lecture, sentinel nodes called header and trailer mark the two ends.

qs.q: In a doubly linked list, a node consists of ____

c.x: A data item and a next pointer only
A previous pointer and a next pointer only
A data item, a next pointer and a previous pointer

e: In a doubly linked list each node keeps an explicit reference to the node before it and to the node after it.
The lecture's _Node class has three fields: _element, _prev and _next.
This lets us delete a node at the tail or in the interior efficiently, which a singly linked list cannot do.

qs.q: The DoublyLinkedList class must maintain a reference to the ____ node.
e: The list must be reachable from both ends: in the lecture this is done with the header (before the first element) and trailer (after the last element) sentinels.
Keeping only one end would make operations on the other end require traversal, and keeping references to all nodes is unnecessary because nodes are linked.

qs.q: True or False: A priority queue operates like any other queue according to the first-in-first-out (FIFO) principle, even when its items have different priority levels.
e: A priority queue removes the element with the first priority (the minimum key), not the one that arrived first.
Example from the lecture: after add(5,A), add(9,C), add(3,B), remove_min() returns (3,B) even though it was inserted last.
So the statement is False.

qs.q: The min heap is a binary heap in which the smallest key is always at the ____
e: Heap-order property (min-heap): every key is greater than or equal to its parent's key, so the minimum is stored at the root.
The root is the front of the heap (index 0 in the array representation), which is why min() runs in $O(1)$.
The rear (last position) holds a leaf, which has no guarantee to be the smallest.

qs.q: A binary heap will allow us both enqueue and dequeue items in ____
e: A heap is a complete binary tree, so its height is $\lfloor \log n \rfloor$.
add (up-heap bubbling) and remove_min (down-heap bubbling) perform at most one swap per level, i.e. at most $\lfloor \log n \rfloor$ swaps.
So both operations take $O(\log n)$, better than the list-based priority queues where one of them is $O(n)$.

qs.q: In a ____, the logical order of items inside a queue is determined by their priority.
e: In a priority queue each element is added with a key and the element with the minimum key (highest priority) is removed first, regardless of insertion order.
A stack orders by LIFO and an ordinary queue by FIFO.
